=== page: choices/index.html
title: Choices — The Future of Case Management IT
description: The least conventional decisions in the design, what each is for, and what it costs.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations
Parameters
Choices
Choices
Several decisions here are not what a team would reach for by default. Each is set out with what it buys and what it costs, so that a reader can disagree with it specifically.
01 Store dated claims, not facts –
Why it is unusual
Most case systems store the current value of a field and log changes separately.
What it is for
Whether a person owes money back depends on whether the ministry knew something and failed to act. A current value with a change log beside it cannot answer that reliably, because the log is not part of the decision path.
What it costs
Every read is more complex. Developers have to think in periods rather than values, and reporting has to specify which point in time it means.
02 Track two kinds of time, and inherit a third +
Why it is unusual
Bitemporal modelling is well established in finance and rare in case management.
What it is for
The two questions a tribunal asks are what was true and what the ministry knew. They need separate axes. The third axis exists only because fifteen years of records arrive from a system that is still running, and collapsing their history into the migration date would make an entire class of question unanswerable.
What it costs
More storage, and a real learning curve. The third axis will be unknown in most inherited records, and the system has to say so rather than guess.
03 Five case models rather than one +
Why it is unusual
The conventional move is a single configurable case model shared across programs.
What it is for
A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal share almost nothing. A shared model makes every change a negotiation, and the previous programme cut scope rather than change one.
What it costs
Plumbing gets written five times. This is a real cost and it is accepted deliberately.
04 Decisions read no live data +
Why it is unusual
Rules engines are usually called as a service that fetches what it needs while it runs.
What it is for
If a decision reads anything not stored with it, it cannot be reproduced. Reproduction is the difference between showing a tribunal what happened and reconstructing it from memory.
What it costs
The facts have to be assembled before the decision runs, and assembling them consistently is its own problem.
05 The interface outlives its implementation +
Why it is unusual
Translation layers over a legacy system are normally treated as the durable asset.
What it is for
Replacing a system in pieces only works if consumers are insulated from which piece is answering. The published interface is permanent; the translation layer behind it is temporary and its team is accountable for disbanding.
What it costs
It requires refusing legacy vocabulary in the published interface even when exposing it would be faster.
06 Store the letter, not just the decision +
Why it is unusual
Correspondence is usually treated as output rather than part of the record.
What it is for
A tribunal asks what the person was told as often as it asks what was computed. A determination that reproduces perfectly alongside an unreconstructable letter does not answer the question.
What it costs
Template versions and content hashes have to be retained for as long as the decisions that reference them.
07 Retention lives on the type, not the storage location +
Why it is unusual
Retention is commonly inferred from where something is stored.
What it is for
Inference from location fails the first time a fact appears in two places, which is the first day. Attaching classification and retention to the kind of evidence makes disposition tractable.
What it costs
Every evidence type needs a records determination before it can be used, which puts the records office on the critical path.
How the design was arrived at
This architecture rests on an analysis of every document that could be recovered about ICM and the business processes it supports. Each claim is traceable to a primary source, confirmed internally, or derived by arithmetic. Unverified claims are marked as such rather than quietly asserted.
The design began with the assumptions that underpinned ICM and much of the approach to MIS. Eleven were tested and none survived intact. Two of them:
System residency is a legal requirement
Neither federal nor provincial statute requires government systems to be located in Canada, and no published policy requires it either.
Concerns about data sovereignty and trade point toward Canadian residency, and the architecture follows that. There is no formal guidance behind it.
Replacing the existing system has a deadline
Vendor support for the current platform is committed through at least December 2037, on a rolling ten-year basis.
Nothing external forces the replacement to finish by a particular date. The programme can run discovery, research and analysis properly before committing to large-scale development, and an unforced timetable takes a great deal of risk out of deployment.
Two of the eleven assumptions that did not survive testing.
What the evidence base is
Two bodies of source material sit behind this: the 57 technical design documents for the current release of the existing system, covering the application, its integrations, its data conversion and its reporting; and the 326 service-delivery procedures describing how the work is done.
Reading both matters, because they disagree about what the system is. The technical documents describe 61 applications. The procedures reveal 28 further tools that a worker actually touches and that appear in no technical document: a standalone calculator, a reporting tool, credit and asset-check portals, a worker-safety device, a vital statistics service.
What remains unresolved
The architecture carries 40 open verification items and 30 items that must be resolved before the design is frozen. Three are worth naming here because they change the shape of the work rather than its detail:
Whether the rules can be migrated independently of the mainframe, given that both calculate.
Whether the decision on what the third time axis holds can be made before the first production record is written. It cannot be added afterwards.
What service levels the analytical platform can commit to, which depends on a storage benchmark that has not yet been run.
DRAFT
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.

Current State
This design is not a contradiction of the current system. It comes out of asking why a large, expensive piece of software, laboured over by hundreds of intelligent, well-intentioned, capable people, can still fail the organizations it is meant to serve. The answer lies in what the system leaves out: what it ignores, and what it pushes outside itself.
What the SDPR procedures are
Every recurring task a caseworker performs has a written procedure: what starts it, which screens to open, which form to send, what to type in which field. Together they run to 8.2 million characters. They describe the service as it is actually delivered.
Each one carries a header naming its purpose, the policy it implements, the legislation behind it, and how the work is classified in the system. That makes the whole set readable as a map of the services.
326procedures
15capability areas
128kinds of work request
84statutory provisions cited
146distinct forms
13ways to reach the ministry
Work crosses system boundaries constantly
63% of documented procedures need two or more systems to finish one task.
Number of procedures by count of separate systems required, across 326 procedures.
Systems
Procedures
Proportion
0
39
1
80
2
114
3
51
4+
42
Highlighted rows are the 207 procedures that cross a system boundary. Four procedures require seven.
Counted by naming every system referenced in each procedure. The most common pairing is the Siebel case system with the client portal, then the case system with Service Canada, then the case system with the mainframe.
One journey, three systems, two re-keys
Recovering an overpayment is the clearest example. A worker who has decided that someone was paid too much must:
Open a separate web application to calculate the amount. It does not connect to either system of record.
Print the result, scan it, and attach it back to the case.
Move the case file to their own office in the mainframe so they have permission to act on it.
Type the amount into the mainframe by hand.
Move the case file back to where it came from.
For clients whose earnings are annualised there is a further step: a spreadsheet, with figures read off one screen, typed into the spreadsheet, and the result typed back.
None of this is anyone's poor practice. It is written down as the correct procedure, because given the systems that exist it is the correct procedure.
Where the rules actually live
A modernisation needs to know what it is replacing. The rules that decide entitlement are in four separate places, and only one of them is a rules engine.
Business rules by location
Where
What it holds
A rules engine
29 separate rulebases covering eligibility, validation, debt and payment calculation
The mainframe
Benefit calculation, rate recalculation, time limits, sanction end dates
Formulas inside the case system
Retention periods, access levels, privacy calculations
A database table
The rates the public-facing eligibility estimator uses
Found by reading the technical design documents for the current release alongside the procedures. No source control, promotion pipeline or version register is documented for the 29 rulebases.
Routing runs on a spreadsheet
Which queue a request joins, how urgent it is, how long it has, and where a scanned document goes are all defined in an Excel workbook that 56 procedures refer to. One of its sheets maps 445 form numbers to their handling. Priority and service-level targets for the whole service sit outside the platform, maintained by hand.
Accommodation and the signature problem
There is a path for applicants who need an interpreter, find reading difficult, or have limited computer access: a worker reads the questions aloud and enters the answers for them.
Because that path skips portal registration, no personal identification number is created for the applicant. The electronic signature depends on that number. The people the accommodation exists for are the people who cannot then sign electronically.
How these figures were produced
The counts come from reading the Resource Finder and the other document repositories in full, then pattern-matching and mapping the text. Named systems, capability areas and the policy behind each procedure come from the documents and the policy manual.
Volumes are not yet measured. Caseload throughput, worker streams, transaction rates and queue depth can all be counted directly; the figures here were taken from the technical design documents instead.
The rest of the site sets out how the design answers these conditions. The clearest place to see the connection is evidence, because the overpayment journey above is a direct consequence of a record that cannot say what was known and when.

=== page: determinations/index.html
title: Determinations — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why an entitlement decision is treated as a function that can be re-run years later.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations
Parameters
Choices
Determinations
A decision about someone's entitlement may be challenged years after it was made. The design treats every decision as something that can be re-run rather than remembered.
The problem with asking a system what it decided
Ask a typical case management system why a person received a particular amount in March 2022 and it will recalculate. It will use today's rules, today's data and today's software, and report the answer with confidence. That answer may be right. There is no way to tell, and no way to show a tribunal the difference.
Three things have moved underneath since March 2022. Policy changed. The person's recorded circumstances changed, possibly several times. The software itself was upgraded, and a rules engine upgrade can alter how the same rule evaluates without anyone noticing until someone appeals.
Treating a decision as a function
The design makes entitlement a calculation with no hidden inputs. It reads the rules, the facts and the date it is deciding for. It does not read the clock, does not query a database, and does not call another service while it runs. Everything it needs is handed to it.
That constraint sounds academic. It is what makes the next part possible: if nothing hidden went in, then storing what went in is enough to reproduce what came out.
The function signature
Determine(rulesArtefactVersion, evidenceSnapshot, referenceDate) → DeterminationResult
Pure: no input or output, no clock reads, no database access, no service calls. No rules engine provides this on its own; it is enforced by the shell around the engine. The engine evaluates in-process against a snapshot passed by value, which is what makes byte-identical replay achievable rather than aspirational.
Five things stored with every decision
Storing the answer is not enough, and storing the answer plus the rules is still not enough. Five artefacts are bound into the record at the moment the decision is made.
1 The rules Content digest, tagged and immutable once released Stored
2 The engine Version number and the archived binary Stored
3 The facts it saw Copied in full into the record, never referenced Stored
4 The reasoning Which rules fired and which branches were taken, in a ministry-owned format Stored
5 The letter Content-hashed template, resolved at decision time Stored
The decision can be replayed.
Four years on, the same inputs produce the same answer, the reasoning can be read aloud, and the letter the client received can be reproduced.
Switch any artefact off to see which question stops being answerable. Each one covers a failure the other four do not.
The fifth is the one most often left out. A determination that reproduces perfectly, paired with a letter nobody can reconstruct, does not answer the question a tribunal actually put, which is frequently about what the person was told rather than what the system computed.
How long replay has to work
Archiving the software guarantees you can identify it. It does not guarantee that anything in twenty years can run it. The operating system, the processor architecture and the container runtime all have shorter lives than a child protection record, which is retained for ninety years.
Rather than leave that unresolved, the design commits to a horizon in three stages and writes it down in advance.
Years 0–7
The software itself is archived and tested quarterly to confirm it still runs. Seven years covers the appeal, reconsideration and audit paths that actually re-execute.
Years 7–20
The rules are maintained as a written specification, with a test suite that any re-implementation must reproduce. The suite is kept independent of the engine from the first day, so this transition costs nothing when it arrives.
Beyond 20 years
The stored reasoning, the letter and the facts are the record, and re-running is no longer offered. This is what a paper file has always been.
The three stages run in order, which is why they are numbered. The last is defensible because it was declared in advance rather than discovered during a hearing.
Two decisions made moments apart can disagree
Storing the inputs makes replay reliable. It says nothing about whether the inputs were gathered consistently, and that is where the remaining gap sits.
Assembling the facts means reading across several stores that update independently. Two decisions issued seconds apart, where one store is briefly behind, can legitimately see different worlds. Both replay perfectly. Both are reproducible. They disagree, and nothing described so far detects it. The design pins each snapshot to a point in the sequence of recorded events, so a later reader can tell which view of the world a decision was made against.
Decisions that affect people carry their own classification
Every rule is labelled with what kind of decision it produces: an administrative decision that requires reasons, a decision that a person must make before it takes effect, or an intermediate calculation that affects nobody on its own.
That label travels with the decision into the letter. An adverse determination emits its reasons, its appeal period and the route to challenge it because the classification says it must, not because somebody remembered.

=== page: domains/index.html
title: Domains — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why the design uses sixteen separate models rather than one, and the rules that keep them separate.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations
Parameters
Choices
Domains
Perhaps the most consequential choice in this design is where to draw the lines between parts of the system. Twelve domain models, one of which is really five sub-domains, which makes sixteen.
The problem of a single model
Programmes like this usually begin by building one model of a case that every program can share. That is how MIS began, and how ICM began. It looks like the responsible choice: less duplication, one place to change things, consistency across the ministry.
What happens next is well documented. A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal have almost nothing in common beyond involving a person. Making them share a lifecycle means every change to one is negotiated with everyone else. Multiply that over dozens of programs and the model becomes something nobody can change. So sub-entities get bolted on and extended, and integration patterns multiply. The system becomes a plate of spaghetti: nothing can be changed in one place, and any failure reaches everywhere. This is not hypothetical. ICM merged its final two phases and cut child protection scope for exactly this reason.
This design takes the difference seriously. Five program families get five case models. The plumbing is written more than once, and that is cheaper than the alternative.
What the parts are
Shared spine
Participant Identity
Evidence & Verification
Eligibility & Entitlement
One per program family
Employment assistance
Child protection
Child care subsidy
Employment services
Persons with disabilities
Money
Payments & Issuance
Financial Components
Overpayment & Recovery
Delivery
Appeals & Reconsideration
Work Management
Documents & Capture
Notices & Correspondence
Provider & Outcome
Evidence & Verification
Every dated claim about the world, and how it was checked.
Owns
The evidence succession set, verification policy, the four operations, three time axes.
Does not own
It does not decide anything. It records what was claimed and what was verified.
Boundary test
Its events are the trigger fabric for everything else.
Select any part to see what it owns, what it deliberately does not own, and the test that tells you when the boundary has been breached. The five case models share protocols, not a case model.
Four rules keep the lines in place
A boundary that exists only in a diagram will not survive delivery pressure. These are written so that a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies.
Each part can be released on its own
It has its own storage and its own message topics. If two parts always have to ship together, they are one part wearing two names.
No part reads another part's database
No shared tables. No joins across schemas. Not for a report, and not in a test environment. This is the rule that erodes first and takes the longest to notice.
There are exactly two ways to talk
A published interface for reads, and published events for notifications. There is no third mechanism, and adding one is not a shortcut.
Copies are owned by whoever holds them
A part needing another's data keeps its own copy, built from that part's events, shaped the way it needs. When the source corrects something, the copy has to follow.
The thin identity model
Participant Identity is deliberately small: identifiers, enough detail to tell two people apart, and whether identity has been proven. Not addresses, not income, not relationships.
This is the part most likely to drift, because every new requirement produces a reason to add one more field to the person record. Once that starts, the shared model has been rebuilt in the one place the design most needs to stay thin.
Merge and split are built in from the first day rather than added later. The previous system's audit found duplicate records at scale, with search described as ineffective and exact-match only. Retrofitting merge into a system that assumed one person equals one row is close to impossible, because by then every payment instruction and every stored decision has keyed itself to an identifier the design promised would be stable.
Published events and the boundary test
Participant Identity publishes PersonRegistered, IdentityMerged, IdentitySplit, IdentifierAdded and IdentifierInvalidated. Every other context maintains its own projection (Payee, Applicant, Caregiver, Reporter, Appellant, Debtor) keyed by participant identifier.
Evidence & Verification publishes EvidenceRecorded, EvidenceActivated, EvidenceSuperseded, EvidenceVerified, EvidenceInvalidated and EvidenceCorrectionRecorded.
Parts that are not domain models
Some pieces are shared infrastructure rather than parts of the business. They are owned by platform teams and used by everyone. The distinction matters because a platform part that starts holding program state has quietly become a seventeenth domain model without anyone chartering it.
Two of them are worth naming, because their charters are deliberately opposite. The published interface is permanent: it is the contract built to outlive the systems that implement it. The translation layer over the existing Siebel system is temporary, and the team that builds it is accountable for its own disbandment.
A team accountable for a thing will grow and protect it. A team measured on its own dissolution will not.

=== page: evidence/index.html
title: Evidence — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why the system records dated claims rather than facts, and why it tracks two kinds of time.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations

Evidence
ICM tracks facts. Fields are overwritten and history is obscured. In the new system the unit of information is a timestamped, attributable claim linked to evidence. That claim can be disproved, confirmed, overturned or replaced, and no information is lost on the way.
Why not store facts?
A system that stores only the current state, "Income: $900", leaves the important questions unanswered. How do we know? What evidence is there? When did we know? Is this the corrected number, or the number recorded at the time?
Front-line staff adapt, so the information is not lost. It is just not modelled. It goes into notes, forms and attachments, and only a thin slice of it is ever held as data.
This is not an auditing nicety. It closes the gap between how the system holds data and how front-line staff work. Substantiating evidence against claims is the most common task a worker performs, and the system does not model it at all, so it is done by hand. Social workers spend hours mapping their notes onto a structure that serves the software rather than their clients.
So the unit of storage is an assertion:
what household composition: couple
about whomparticipant 4471-A
true forfrom 1 January, open-ended
learned on12 September
fromeligibility review finding
verifiedtenancy agreement, 14 September
One evidence assertion, from a case where the dates are contested. The ministry now says the household was a couple from January. It came to that view in September. Eight months of payments were made at the single rate in between, and which of those two dates you read decides what happens next.
The four things that can happen to an assertion
Once something is recorded it is never edited in place. Four operations change what the system believes, and they differ in one respect: what each does to the period the claim covers.
[aria-label] Evidence operations
Record
Supersede
Correct
Invalidate
The world changed.
valid time
a new period
transaction time
now
The earlier assertion stays true for its own period. The new one takes over from a later date.
For example A partner moves in on 1 May, and the client reports it.
If this produced an overpayment, the classification rule reads the operation as the world having changed.
Select an operation. Supersede and Correct both replace an earlier claim, but only Correct says the earlier claim was wrong about its own period. That is what separates a recoverable debt from the ministry's own error.
That distinction is the reason the model exists. It is a policy rule expressed in the shape of the data, and it can be applied consistently because the operation that produced a recalculation is recorded on the record itself rather than inferred afterwards.
The operation is an input to the classification rather than the whole of it. Who caused the error matters too, and a client who concealed a relationship is not in the same position as a worker who mis-keyed a figure. What the model guarantees is narrower and more useful: the question is answerable at all, from the record, rather than reconstructed by whoever is looking at the file today.
Where a conventional record gives up
Take the assertion above to a tribunal. The client accepts a relationship exists but disputes that it began in January. Three separate things are now in question, and they are easy to confuse:
What the ministry believed about the household in each of those eight months.
When the ministry changed its mind, and on what evidence.
What start date the ministry now asserts.
A conventional design holds one relationship start date and an audit entry recording that a worker changed it on 12 September. That answers the third question, gestures at the second, and cannot answer the first at all. The eight monthly payments are left looking like errors, when at the time each was the correct application of what was then known.
The operations, formally
Operation
Valid time
Transaction time
Meaning
RecordEvidence
asserted period
now
We learned a new fact
SupersedeEvidence
new period
now
The world changed
CorrectEvidence
same period
now
We were wrong about the world
InvalidateEvidence
closed
now
The assertion should never have existed
The aggregate is the evidence succession set: the stream of versions of one logical fact about one subject. Commands append events; current state is a projection. Verification status transitions are themselves events.
The third date, and the history problem
Two time axes are standard. This design carries a third, and it exists because the new system inherits fifteen years of records from systems that are still running.
When old records are brought across, they all arrive on the same day. If that migration date becomes the "when we learned it" date for every inherited record, then every historical fact appears to have been learned simultaneously. Supersede and Correct become indistinguishable across the whole pre-cutover record, and the overpayment classification rule cannot run against the records where most overpayments actually sit.
The third axis holds the date the predecessor system asserted the fact, where that can be read out of the old record. It is frequently unknowable, so it carries a confidence marker, and where the answer is unknown the system says so rather than guessing.
valid time
The period in the world for which the fact holds.
Set by whoever asserts it, from the source.
transaction time
When this system learned it.
Set at recording. Never changes.
legacy assertion time
When the previous system asserted it, if that can be decoded.
Set at migration. Often unknown, and marked as such.
Three dates on every assertion. The third is nullable; the design treats an unknown value as unknown rather than substituting the migration date.
This cannot be added later. Events are immutable: a field can be introduced with a default, but it cannot be filled in retroactively, because the source was either decoded at migration or it was not. The decision has to be made before the first production record is written.
Confidence values and replay behaviour
legacy_asserted_at is accompanied by legacy_assertion_confidence, which takes DECODED (read directly from the legacy record or audit trail), INFERRED (derived from a related artefact by a documented rule) or UNKNOWN.
On UNKNOWN, any consumer computing a knowledge-state answer (the overpayment classification rule, a tribunal reconstruction view, a disclosure history) must return INDETERMINATE. Projections that answer only valid-time questions ignore the field.
Retroactive recalculation runs off valid time, which a competent migration preserves, so recalculation is unaffected. What breaks without the third axis is narrower: what the ministry knew and when, which is the question separating a recoverable debt from the ministry's own error.

A PWD* designation granted in July.
It takes effect from March.
Four months of payments were correct when they were made, and are now an underpayment: four months a client went without money they turn out to have been entitled to. The current system keeps only today's answer, rewriting history rather than recording it. What did we know, when did we know it, and how can that be proven? The design on these pages keeps all three.

Asked in Jun about May, the system reports a monthly entitlement of $1,060.
Current version of the record: At application in March, no disability designation is in place.
Today the system reports $1,535.50 for May. The payment actually made that month was correct when it was issued, and is now an underpayment of $475.50.
Move either slider. The left one changes the month you are asking about. The right one changes the month you are asking in. The hard horizontal edge is the July decision reaching back over every month before it, which is what a retroactive determination looks like when both axes are kept.
Current State
Case management covers a wide range of services across the Ministries of Children and Family Development and Social Development and Poverty Reduction. Assistance payments, service requests, social work, loss recovery and client support all depend on a worker having the full context in front of them. The work is life-critical: a wrong answer means someone might not eat this month, or a child misses a check-in.
Two systems do the work: an Oracle Siebel customer relationship management application adapted for government, and a mainframe dating from 1982. They run in parallel and together administer the core programs. Every attempt to retire the mainframe has been abandoned or has failed.
The New Design is Built on Three Pillars
Evidence, not 'facts'
The system will not store "this person is an adult." It stores, "on 14 July, AI Agent ID-33422 read the uploaded image of identification and determined the identity to match the case and the date of birth to be April 22, 1988. Business rules determine they're an adult." Who or what decided, when, and on what basis are part of the record, rather than sitting in an attached PDF or outside the system altogether.
Evidence
Apt boundaries
Two ministries with broad mandates carry a very diverse portfolio. The current system forces all of it into one rigid model, which is how a design becomes brittle. Each program family gets its own model instead.
Domains
A decision you can re-run
Every entitlement decision stores the rules, the engine, the facts it saw, its own reasoning and outcomes. Four days later for a manager or years later at a tribunal, the decision can be replayed rather than reconstructed from memory.
Determinations
Why do backdates matter?
Case management is largely the work of building a consistent timeline as information arrives. It does not arrive in order, and what turns up later can change what earlier events meant. In the retroactive designation above, the client spent four months short of what they were owed, and someone on assistance has no reserve to absorb that. The same machinery runs in the other direction, and lands on the same person, who has to pay the overage back.
When someone is paid more than they were entitled to, the money is treated one of two ways. If the client's circumstances changed and they reported it late, it is a recoverable overpayment, and the ministry takes it back at $10 a month out of a payment that was already only just enough. If the ministry already held the information and did not act on it, that is administrative error, and the client should not be the one carrying it.
Telling those apart requires knowing when the ministry knew. That is a transaction-time question. A system that records only when a fact was true, or that stamps every migrated record with the date it was migrated, cannot answer it. The existing overpayment backlog sits almost entirely in records from before any cutover.
Mispayment is one example of many. Nearly every claim a client makes has to be corroborated by evidence, and that cycle of claim, evidence and substantiation is the core loop of how assistance is administered.
How this is modelled
Every evidence assertion carries three time dimensions: valid_time (the period in the world for which the fact holds), recorded_at (when this system learned it), and legacy_asserted_at (when the predecessor system asserted it, where that can be decoded from the legacy record).
The third axis is nullable and carries a confidence enumeration of DECODED, INFERRED or UNKNOWN. On UNKNOWN, any consumer computing a knowledge-state answer must return INDETERMINATE rather than silently substituting the migration timestamp.
None of this can be added later. Events are immutable, so a field can be added with a default but cannot be populated retroactively. The axis has to exist before the first production event is written.
What this site covers
These pages set out the domain model and the reasoning behind the least conventional choices. Each carries a plain English explanation, with the technical statement behind a disclosure.
Current State is worth reading first if you do not know ICM and MIS, because the design makes most sense against what it replaces. Parameters lists the twenty-one rules the design has to hold to, each with the check that catches a breach.
DRAFT
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.
Figures on this site are drawn from the architecture document and from 326 service-delivery procedures. Nothing here is a government commitment.

Parameters
Twenty-one rules the design has to hold to. Each is written so a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies, and six of them cannot be added once the work has started.
What a parameter is
A parameter is a property a compliant system has, stated with the check that catches its absence. It is not a commitment and not an aspiration. The difference shows up in the wording: every entry below ends in a question a reviewer can put to a running system and get a wrong answer to.
The architecture states twelve. Testing them found three faults. Two said the same thing in different words. Two carried two ideas each, either of which could be dropped without the other. And one gap the architecture names in its own text was held by nothing. The set below fixes each of those, and adds seven more rules on top.
Three claims are made for it. Each parameter is necessary: remove it and the design loses a property nothing else supplies. No two overlap: no property is asserted twice. Together they carry what the architecture is trying to achieve. The first two are demonstrated for each entry. The third is argued against a list of intents, and it is the weakest of the three, because a different architect would reasonably draw some of these lines elsewhere.
The set

N07
The calculation reads nothing but its inputs
No clock, no database, no service calls inside the decision. Everything it needs is handed to it, and the record it writes is a result of the decision, never an input to it.
Why it cannot be dropped
Purity is what makes an identical re-run physically achievable rather than aspirational. A rules service that fetches what it needs gives every decision a dependency on a running system, which is the first thing a tribunal will probe.
The test that fails
Given the same rules, the same engine version and the same inputs, does it produce a byte-identical trace, with no reference to the clock, the environment or any service?
Where it came from
From P8, narrowed to the calculation
Cannot be added later
The engine must be sealed before the first rule is written
Grouped by the axis each one occupies. Select any parameter for the check that catches a breach. A heavy left edge marks the six that cannot be added later.
Six cannot be added later
Most of these can be satisfied late, at a price. Six cannot. Each describes a property that has to exist before a particular first event, and once that event has happened the fix is a rebuild rather than a repair.
Before the first rule is written N07
The engine is sealed off from live data. A rule authored against a service it can call has already fixed the shape of every rule after it.
Before the first event is written N12, and the third date in N01
How records are destroyed is decided per class of fact. Events are immutable, so a date can be added with a default but never filled in afterwards.
As the first copy is made N06, N21
Where a copy came from, and what its source bars it from, are written at the moment of copying. Neither can be reconstructed later.
From the first decision N09
The point in the event sequence a decision read from goes into its record. Earlier decisions cannot be tied to a consistent view of the world.
Before the first group of clients moves N14
Moving them back is proven rather than claimed, and what the return trip loses is written down and approved.
The gates in the order delivery reaches them. This is a statement about the order the work has to happen in, not about which rules matter most.
Do first only what cannot be done later.
Where the twenty-one came from
Every principle in the architecture is accounted for. Seven were carried across with their wording narrowed or extended, three were split because they held two separable ideas, one absorbed a clause from another, and one was generalised. Twelve principles became fourteen parameters, and seven more were added.
P1 split N01 · N02
P2 narrowed N08
P3 split N03 · N06
P4 absorbs P3(a) N03
P5 carried N04
P6 extended N11
P7 carried N10
P8 narrowed N07
P9 carried N05
P10 generalised N18
P11 split N12 · N13
P12 carried N14
Added N09 · N15 · N16 · N17 · N19 · N20 · N21
N09 closes a gap the architecture identifies in its own text. N15 and N16 close two it had already recorded against itself. The remaining four came out of the policy manual, which turned out to state rules the architecture had not reached.
Those last four are the interesting ones, because nobody found them by thinking harder about the architecture. They came out of reading what the ministry already tells its own staff to do. Policy sets time limits whose breach changes what a client is owed, names which entitlements can be appealed and to whom, separates the person who decides from the person who reviews, and bars certain uses of information the ministry may lawfully hold. None of that was expressible in the twelve.
A rule nobody can check is not a rule
One parameter is not about the system at all. N18 ranges over the other twenty and requires each to name how its breach is caught, with anything expressible as a lint rule or a compatibility check built as one.
It is stated separately rather than folded into the others, because a rule about enforcement filed among rules about behaviour is how enforcement stops being anybody's job without anyone deciding that it should.
What the set does not settle
Three things are open, and they are recorded rather than smoothed over.
Continuity has no footing in policy
N16 asks for recovery targets per service, proven by exercise. Of 270 policy obligations mapped, none exercises it. A benefits platform plainly needs recovery objectives, so that is not evidence the rule is unnecessary. It is evidence that its authority sits somewhere other than the policy manual, and until that source is named the rule stays proposed rather than baselined.
Whether to build this at all
N11 says generic capability is bought and a decision to build is checked by someone other than the builder. At component level the architecture answers the question, though the answer is given by each component's own owner. At platform level it does not answer it: custom build against a commercial case management product is examined nowhere in the source's 4,998 lines. By the architecture's own rule that is a compliance failure rather than a matter of taste, and it is the largest open question on this page.
The premise underneath the decision model
Everything on the determinations page rests on the premise that entitlement decisions can be expressed as functions of recorded evidence. Review conceded that the premise may be false for some decisions. It drives roughly 28% of programme cost and appears in no assumption register. It belongs in one.
What the set is checked against
Sufficiency is argued against an enumerated register of what the architecture is trying to achieve. An intent with no parameter is a sufficiency failure; a parameter carrying no intent is a necessity failure.

Cuts a reviewer could reasonably reopen
Four places where the set could have been drawn differently, recorded so that reopening one is a deliberate act rather than a rediscovery.
N01 and N02. The architecture bundles these as one principle with one test. A reviewer who holds that the rule on payloads follows from the model of a fact would merge them, giving twenty.
N12 and N13. The split turns on custodianship having a different authority and a different rights holder from disposition. An architect treating Indigenous jurisdiction as one input to a single records design would keep them together.
N09. Arguably a clause of N08 rather than a parameter of its own. It is separate because N08's test cannot detect its breach, and a clause its parent's test cannot see is not enforced.
N15. Merges accessibility and digital exclusion on the grounds of a shared failure mode. An architect who treats them as separate obligations would split it.
The parameters that do most of the work on the rest of this site are N01 on evidence, N03 on domains, and N07 to N09 on determinations. The choices page sets out what several of them cost.

A bar absent at capture is absent from every earlier copy
A boundary that exists only in a diagram will not survive delivery pressure. These are written so that a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies.
A breach is visible rather than professed
A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal share almost nothing. A shared model makes every change a negotiation, and the previous programme cut scope rather than change one.
A client is told the truth about what they may challenge
A conventional design holds one relationship start date and an audit entry recording that a worker changed it on 12 September. That answers the third question, gestures at the second, and cannot answer the first at all. The eight monthly payments are left looking like errors, when at the time each was the correct application of what was then known.
A database table
A decision about someone's entitlement may be challenged years after it was made. The design treats every decision as something that can be re-run rather than remembered.
A decision is defensible at tribunal four years later
A decision stores which rules version ran against which evidence version, and stores the artefacts rather than pointing at them. It also records what was asked for, which criteria were met and which were not, what was assumed, what evidence was missing, and the date the client was told.
A decision you can re-run

A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, explained in plain English.
A document is not evidence.
A document is what a verification policy accepts as satisfying an evidence type. Losing that distinction turns the file store into a second system of record.
A fact is a dated claim with a source
A first assertion about a period nothing covered yet.
A modernisation needs to know what it is replacing. The rules that decide entitlement are in four separate places, and only one of them is a rules engine.
A parameter is a property a compliant system has, stated with the check that catches its absence. It is not a commitment and not an aspiration. The difference shows up in the wording: every entry below ends in a question a reviewer can put to a running system and get a wrong answer to.
A part needing another's data keeps its own copy, built from that part's events, shaped the way it needs. When the source corrects something, the copy has to follow.
A part that copies evidence records where it came from. When the source corrects it, every holder of a copy can be listed and has to act, including where a decision was already made on the old value.
A partner moves in on 1 May, and the client reports it.
A person can reach the same outcome whatever their disability and whichever route they take. Interfaces meet the Province’s accessibility standard at first release, and every journey has a supported route that is not digital.
A pointer resolves to whatever the database says today. Replay returns today’s answer to a four-year-old question.
A pointer to a running system is not evidence: replay has to survive the retirement of everything that produced the decision, including the engine. And the client is owed the record itself, assembled and severed under FOIPPA, which replay alone does not deliver.
A published interface for reads, and published events for notifications. There is no third mechanism, and adding one is not a shortcut.
A review establishes the household was a couple from January, not a single person.
A rule nobody can check is not a rule
A rules engine
A shared model decides whose release everyone else waits for. The previous programme merged its last two phases and cut child protection scope because of exactly this.
A store with no disposition design cannot acquire one afterwards
A system that stores only the current state, "Income: $900", leaves the important questions unanswered. How do we know? What evidence is there? When did we know? Is this the corrected number, or the number recorded at the time?
A team accountable for a thing will grow and protect it. A team measured on its own dissolution will not.
A tribunal asks equally what the client was told.
A tribunal asks what the person was told as often as it asks what was computed. A determination that reproduces perfectly alongside an unreconstructable letter does not answer the question.
Accommodation and the signature problem
Accounts, accruals, schedules, double-entry postings.
Added since the source
All twenty-one
An append-only store and a statutory duty to destroy are in direct tension, and resolving that tension after the first event is a rebuild rather than a repair. The timing is the rule: a correct design arrived at late is a failed one.
An engine upgrade can change how the same rules evaluate.
An entitlement determined twice must not be paid twice, and that guarantee lives here rather than in five case contexts.
Appeals & Reconsideration
Apt boundaries
Archiving the software guarantees you can identify it. It does not guarantee that anything in twenty years can run it. The operating system, the processor architecture and the container runtime all have shorter lives than a child protection record, which is retained for ninety years.
Arguably a clause of N08 rather than a parameter of its own. It is separate because N08's test cannot detect its breach, and a clause its parent's test cannot see is not enforced.
As the first copy is made
Ask a typical case management system why a person received a particular amount in March 2022 and it will recalculate. It will use today's rules, today's data and today's software, and report the answer with confidence. That answer may be right. There is no way to tell, and no way to show a tribunal the difference.
Ask about
Asked in
Assembling the facts means reading across several stores that update independently. Two decisions issued seconds apart, where one store is briefly behind, can legitimately see different worlds. Both replay perfectly. Both are reproducible. They disagree, and nothing described so far detects it. The design pins each snapshot to a point in the sequence of recorded events, so a later reader can tell which view of the world a decision was made against.
Assembling the facts means reading stores that update independently. The decision records the point in the event sequence it read from, sets a limit on how far behind a store may be, and refuses to issue outside that limit.
At application in March, no disability designation is in place.
At application, the client declares they live alone.
Because that path skips portal registration, no personal identification number is created for the applicant. The electronic signature depends on that number. The people the accommodation exists for are the people who cannot then sign electronically.

Before the first group of clients moves
Before the first rule is written
Behaviour lives with the data it governs
Benefit calculation, rate recalculation, time limits, sanction end dates
Beyond 20 years
Bitemporal modelling is well established in finance and rare in case management.
Boundaries and authority
Boundary test
Business rules by location
Can a decision made three years ago be replayed today from storage alone, with nothing running? Can the appeal record be assembled and severed on demand?
Can a reviewer tell from the schema which product implements it? Then remove the product and count the changes to the contract.
Can this group return to the old system today, without a data project, and can you name every class of fact that would not survive the trip? Correction-versus-supersession has no destination in the old system: if that is not on the list, the list is incomplete.
Cannot be added later
Capture, attachment lifecycle, extraction, e-signature, and the link between a document and the claim it supports.
Carried by
Case management covers a wide range of services across the Ministries of Children and Family Development and Social Development and Poverty Reduction. Assistance payments, service requests, social work, loss recovery and client support all depend on a worker having the full context in front of them. The work is life-critical: a wrong answer means someone might not eat this month, or a child misses a check-in.
Case management is largely the work of building a consistent timeline as information arrives. It does not arrive in order, and what turns up later can change what earlier events meant. In the retroactive designation above, the client spent four months short of what they were owed, and someone on assistance has no reserve to absorb that. The same machinery runs in the other direction, and lands on the same person, who has to pay the overage back.
Challenging a decision.

Client-affecting data is never merged by machine
Concerns about data sovereignty and trade point toward Canadian residency, and the architecture follows that. There is no formal guidance behind it.

Documents & Capture
Does any part read another part’s tables, or depend on a type it does not own? The second question catches the failure that actually happens: shared models come back as schemas rather than as databases.
Does not own
Domains — The Future of Case Management IT
Each one carries a header naming its purpose, the policy it implements, the legislation behind it, and how the work is classified in the system. That makes the whole set readable as a map of the services.
Each parameter names how its violation is detected, and any detection that can be written as a lint rule, a fitness function or a compatibility check is written as one.
Each part can be released on its own
Each part keeps its own picture of a person, a case, a payment. No canonical Person, no shared schema, no join across parts, no dependency on a type another part owns.
Effort concentrates on what is distinctive to the ministry
Effort spent building commodity capability is effort not spent on reproducible decisions, which is where the programme will be judged. Without the independent check the test is self-certifying, which is how it currently fails.
Eligibility & Entitlement
Employment assistance
Employment services
Every copy is traceable, and every correction reaches it
Every dated claim about the world, and how it was checked.
Every entitlement decision stores the rules, the engine, the facts it saw, its own reasoning and outcomes. Four days later for a manager or years later at a tribunal, the decision can be replayed rather than reconstructed from memory.
Every evidence assertion carries three time dimensions:
Every evidence type needs a records determination before it can be used, which puts the records office on the critical path.
Every group of clients moved can be moved back without a data project, with an approved statement of what the return trip loses. Reversibility is a property of the mechanism and of the fidelity.
Every principle in the architecture is accounted for. Seven were carried across with their wording narrowed or extended, three were split because they held two separable ideas, one absorbed a clause from another, and one was generalised. Twelve principles became fourteen parameters, and seven more were added.
Every read is more complex. Developers have to think in periods rather than values, and reporting has to specify which point in time it means.
Every recurring task a caseworker performs has a written procedure: what starts it, which screens to open, which form to send, what to type in which field. Together they run to 8.2 million characters. They describe the service as it is actually delivered.
Every rule carries a way of catching a breach
Every rule is labelled with what kind of decision it produces: an administrative decision that requires reasons, a decision that a person must make before it takes effect, or an intermediate calculation that affects nobody on its own.
Every service carries an availability target and stated recovery times, set against what its failure does to a client, and demonstrated by exercise rather than asserted. Shared infrastructure inherits the strictest target of anything that depends on it.
Every step back is possible, and its losses are published
Every step is reversible at known cost
Every time limit is modelled once, with what starts it, how long it runs, which extensions are allowed and who must authorise each. A breach is a recorded event, and where policy attaches a consequence, the system applies it without being asked.

Evidence — The Future of Case Management IT
Evidence, not 'facts'

Financial Components
Five case models rather than one
Five things stored with every decision
For any evidence type: can you state its custodian, and does the system read that rather than people following a convention? Is every access decision traceable to the agreement registry and to no other source?
For clients whose earnings are annualised there is a further step: a spreadsheet, with figures read off one screen, typed into the spreadsheet, and the result typed back.
For each entitlement the system records its statutory basis, whether a decision on it can be reconsidered, whether it can be appealed, and to which body. Recorded per entitlement and per variant, never inferred from the parent programme.
For each journey: can it be completed on every supported channel, and does the outcome change with the route? For each interface: assessed with assistive technology, not only by automated scan, which catches around 30% of issues.
For each parameter, name its detection and say whether it is automated. Where a person checks something a machine could check, say which, and why it has not been automated.
For every custom-built component: which statutory, policy or programme requirement does no commodity option meet, and who other than the builder assessed that answer?
For every entitlement and every variant: can the system state its basis, whether it is reconsiderable, whether it is appealable and to which forum, without inferring any of it from the parent?
For every entitlement, name who holds the deciding capacity and who holds the reviewing one, and state what the ministry retains. Is a decision traceable to the person who reasoned it, as distinct from anyone who advised?
For every limit: modelled once, with its owner, its class, its start event, duration, extensions and authorisations? Is a breach detected without a person noticing it, and its consequence applied automatically?
For every record in transition, name the single system of record and the group it covers. If the answer is “it depends on the field”, the split has been drawn across attributes rather than across groups of clients.
For example
Formulas inside the case system
Found by reading the technical design documents for the current release alongside the procedures. No source control, promotion pipeline or version register is documented for the 29 rulebases.
Four months of payments were correct when they were made, and are now an underpayment: four months a client went without money they turn out to have been entitled to. The current system keeps only today's answer, rewriting history rather than recording it. What did we know, when did we know it, and how can that be proven? The design on these pages keeps all three.
Four or more
Four places where the set could have been drawn differently, recorded so that reopening one is a deliberate act rather than a rediscovery.
Four rules keep the lines in place
Four years on, the same inputs produce the same answer, the reasoning can be read aloud, and the letter the client received can be reproduced.

How long a coexistence runs is controlled elsewhere. How much it loses on the way back is controlled by nothing else, and a rollback plan that does not say what is lost has not been tested.
How long replay has to work
How records are destroyed is decided per class of fact. Events are immutable, so a date can be added with a default but never filled in afterwards.
How records end is decided per class of fact before anything is written: a schedule, an indirection, or destroying one person’s key. What survives a destruction is published, key custody is designed, and the behaviour of a replay that meets an unreadable event is specified.

It does not bend to fit a subsidy renewal.
It does not calculate entitlement.
It does not decide anything. It records what was claimed and what was verified.
It does not disburse.
It has its own storage and its own message topics. If two parts always have to ship together, they are one part wearing two names.
It holds no state of its own between decisions and reads no live data at decision time.
It is stated separately rather than folded into the others, because a rule about enforcement filed among rules about behaviour is how enforcement stops being anybody's job without anyone deciding that it should.
It receives the decision classification so an adverse determination emits reasons and an appeal period by construction.
It requires refusing legacy vocabulary in the published interface even when exposing it would be faster.

Limits on use travel with the information
Logic spread across layers cannot be reasoned about, tested or changed with confidence, and it produces the state where nobody can say which copy is authoritative. It also makes validation uniform: a rule the data enforces cannot be bypassed by an integration or a migration script.
Merge and split are built in from the first day rather than added later. The previous system's audit found duplicate records at scale, with search described as ineffective and exact-match only. Retrofitting merge into a system that assumed one person equals one row is close to impossible, because by then every payment instruction and every stored decision has keyed itself to an identifier the design promised would be stable.
Merges accessibility and digital exclusion on the grounds of a shared failure mode. An architect who treats them as separate obligations would split it.
Mispayment is one example of many. Nearly every claim a client makes has to be corroborated by evidence, and that cycle of claim, evidence and substantiation is the core loop of how assistance is administered.
Modelled once, not per program family. An allowed appeal is a retroactive determination, not a manual adjustment.

N11 says generic capability is bought and a decision to build is checked by someone other than the builder. At component level the architecture answers the question, though the answer is given by each component's own owner. At platform level it does not answer it: custom build against a commercial case management product is examined nowhere in the source's 4,998 lines. By the architecture's own rule that is a compliance failure rather than a matter of taste, and it is the largest open question on this page.

N12, and the third date in N01
N16 asks for recovery targets per service, proven by exercise. Of 270 policy obligations mapped, none exercises it. A benefits platform plainly needs recovery objectives, so that is not evidence the rule is unnecessary. It is evidence that its authority sits somewhere other than the policy manual, and until that source is named the rule stays proposed rather than baselined.

New, from the gaps the architecture records; still proposed
No addresses, no payment details, no employment records, no relationships. Those are evidence, owned elsewhere.
No clock, no database, no service calls inside the decision. Everything it needs is handed to it, and the record it writes is a result of the decision, never an input to it.
No part depends on a model it does not own
No part reads another part's database
No shared tables. No joins across schemas. Not for a report, and not in a test environment. This is the rule that erodes first and takes the longest to notice.
No system named
Nobody can explain the decision in words. It can perhaps be re-run, but it cannot be accounted for.
None of this can be added later. Events are immutable, so a field can be added with a default but cannot be populated retroactively. The axis has to exist before the first production event is written.
None of this is anyone's poor practice. It is written down as the correct procedure, because given the systems that exist it is the correct procedure.
Nothing downstream can be rebuilt without it. A decision cannot be replayed against evidence whose period is unknown, and a correction cannot be told apart from a change in the world.
Nothing else catches a lawfully held fact reaching a use it was barred from. Policy bars five different things: an attribute, a class of content, a counterparty, a subject matter, and an act of communication. Only the first has anything to do with a calculation.
Nothing else in the set detects a system that is correct, reproducible, well-bounded and unreachable by the people it exists for. That failure is invisible in aggregate usage data and falls entirely on clients and front-line staff.
Nothing else makes a recovery obligation detectable. Every recovery figure in the architecture covers the analytics platform. None exists for the published interface, the translation layer, the decision service or the case stores. A missed payment run is not recovered by the system coming back.
Nothing else says who may exercise an authority. The decision record says what was decided and by whom; it does nothing to stop the same person deciding, reviewing and releasing the money. Policy states all three limbs directly.
Nothing external forces the replacement to finish by a particular date. The programme can run discovery, research and analysis properly before committing to large-scale development, and an unforced timetable takes a great deal of risk out of deployment.
Nothing is stored as a bare value. Every fact carries who claimed it, the period it covers, the date this system learned it, and the date the old system asserted it, or a marker saying that date cannot be read.
Nothing on this site is a government commitment, and none of it is a record of any real person.

Published events and the boundary test
Published interfaces use policy and domain words, not the vocabulary of whatever product sits behind them. The interface is the permanent artefact; the translation layer over the existing system is temporary, and its team is chartered to disband.
Pure: no clock, no database, no service calls.
Pure: no input or output, no clock reads, no database access, no service calls. No rules engine provides this on its own; it is enforced by the shell around the engine. The engine evaluates in-process against a snapshot passed by value, which is what makes byte-identical replay achievable rather than aspirational.
Purity is what makes an identical re-run physically achievable rather than aspirational. A rules service that fetches what it needs gives every decision a dependency on a running system, which is the first thing a tribunal will probe.
Rather than leave that unresolved, the design commits to a horizon in three stages and writes it down in advance.
Reach does not depend on the client’s capability or channel

Template versions and content hashes have to be retained for as long as the decisions that reference them.
That constraint sounds academic. It is what makes the next part possible: if nothing hidden went in, then storing what went in is enough to reproduce what came out.
That distinction is the reason the model exists. It is a policy rule expressed in the shape of the data, and it can be applied consistently because the operation that produced a recalculation is recorded on the record itself rather than inferred afterwards.
That label travels with the decision into the letter. An adverse determination emits its reasons, its appeal period and the route to challenge it because the classification says it must, not because somebody remembered.
The Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act commits the Province to alignment, and a Nation’s governance over its own data is not expressible as a retention rule or an access list. A PDF agreement cannot generate an access right, and a right generated anywhere else cannot be audited.

The New Design is Built on Three Pillars
The aggregate is the evidence succession set: the stream of versions of one logical fact about one subject. Commands append events; current state is a projection. Verification status transitions are themselves events.
The architecture bundles these as one principle with one test. A reviewer who holds that the rule on payloads follows from the model of a fact would merge them, giving twenty.
The architecture carries 40 open verification items and 30 items that must be resolved before the design is frozen. Three are worth naming here because they change the shape of the work rather than its detail:
The architecture states the hole in its own text: two decisions issued microseconds apart, one store briefly behind, can legitimately see different worlds. Both replay. Both are reproducible. They disagree, and nothing else notices.
The architecture states twelve. Testing them found three faults. Two said the same thing in different words. Two carried two ideas each, either of which could be dropped without the other. And one gap the architecture names in its own text was held by nothing. The set below fixes each of those, and adds seven more rules on top.

The design makes entitlement a calculation with no hidden inputs. It reads the rules, the facts and the date it is deciding for. It does not read the clock, does not query a database, and does not call another service while it runs. Everything it needs is handed to it.

The rules
The rules are maintained as a written specification, with a test suite that any re-implementation must reproduce. The suite is kept independent of the engine from the first day, so this transition costs nothing when it arrives.

The set
The set is otherwise a statement of intent. Detectability is the prior condition and automation is what follows from it. A rule whose breach nobody can see gets abandoned without anyone deciding to abandon it.
The shape of the payload is what carries provenance across. A row arrives stripped of who claimed it, so the receiver cannot know what it is entitled to conclude, and a later correction has nothing to attach to.

The three stages run in order, which is why they are numbered. The last is defensible because it was declared in advance rather than discovered during a hearing.
The twenty-one rules the design has to hold to, each with the test that catches a breach, and the six that cannot be added later.
The two questions a tribunal asks are what was true and what the ministry knew. They need separate axes. There are exactly two ways to talk
There is a path for applicants who need an interpreter, find reading difficult, or have limited computer access: a worker reads the questions aloud and enters the answers for them.
These pages set out the domain model and the reasoning behind the least conventional choices. Each carries a plain English explanation, with the technical statement behind a disclosure.
This architecture rests on an analysis of every document that could be recovered about ICM and the business processes it supports. Each claim is traceable to a primary source, confirmed internally, or derived by arithmetic. Unverified claims are marked as such rather than quietly asserted.
This cannot be added later. Events are immutable: a field can be introduced with a default, but it cannot be filled in retroactively, because the source was either decoded at migration or it was not. The decision has to be made before the first production record is written.
This design is not a contradiction of the current system. It comes out of asking why a large, expensive piece of software, laboured over by hundreds of intelligent, well-intentioned, capable people, can still fail the organizations it is meant to serve. The answer lies in what the system leaves out: what it ignores, and what it pushes outside itself.
This design takes the difference seriously. Five program families get five case models. The plumbing is written more than once, and that is cheaper than the alternative.
This is an internal working draft. Sign in with your government account to read it.
This is not an auditing nicety. It closes the gap between how the system holds data and how front-line staff work. Substantiating evidence against claims is the most common task a worker performs, and the system does not model it at all, so it is done by hand. Social workers spend hours mapping their notes onto a structure that serves the software rather than their clients.
This is the duty copying creates and nothing else discharges. A design that propagates nothing at all passes every boundary rule perfectly and still leaves people paid on a value known to be wrong.
This is the part most likely to drift, because every new requirement produces a reason to add one more field to the person record. Once that starts, the shared model has been rebuilt in the one place the design most needs to stay thin.
This is what a decision-maker reads out at a hearing.
This is what makes replacement in pieces possible at all. The interface published today over the old platform is the interface published tomorrow over the new services. Conflating the contract with the layer binds legacy vocabulary to the future architecture, which is the failure the programme exists to reverse.
Those last four are the interesting ones, because nobody found them by thinking harder about the architecture. They came out of reading what the ministry already tells its own staff to do. Policy sets time limits whose breach changes what a client is owed, names which entitlements can be appealed and to whom, separates the person who decides from the person who reviews, and bars certain uses of information the ministry may lawfully hold. None of that was expressible in the twelve.
Three claims are made for it. Each parameter is necessary: remove it and the design loses a property nothing else supplies. No two overlap: no property is asserted twice. Together they carry what the architecture is trying to achieve. The first two are demonstrated for each entry. The third is argued against a list of intents, and it is the weakest of the three, because a different architect would reasonably draw some of these lines elsewhere.
Three dates on every assertion. The third is nullable; the design treats an unknown value as unknown rather than substituting the migration date.
Three systems
Three things are open, and they are recorded rather than smoothed over.
Three things have moved underneath since March 2022. Policy changed. The person's recorded circumstances changed, possibly several times. The software itself was upgraded, and a rules engine upgrade can alter how the same rule evaluates without anyone noticing until someone appeals.
To see how one business rule works, how many systems must you open? If more than one, name which is authoritative, why the others exist, and show what generates them.

Treating a decision as a function
Twenty-one rules the design has to hold to. Each is written so a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies, and six of them cannot be added once the work has started.
Two bodies of source material sit behind this: the 57 technical design documents for the current release of the existing system, covering the application, its integrations, its data conversion and its reporting; and the 326 service-delivery procedures describing how the work is done.
Two decisions made moments apart can disagree
Two ministries with broad mandates carry a very diverse portfolio. The current system forces all of it into one rigid model, which is how a design becomes brittle. Each program family gets its own model instead.
Two of the eleven assumptions that did not survive testing.
Two of them are worth naming, because their charters are deliberately opposite. The published interface is permanent: it is the contract built to outlive the systems that implement it. The translation layer over the existing Siebel system is temporary, and the team that builds it is accountable for its own disbandment.
Two systems
Two systems do the work: an Oracle Siebel customer relationship management application adapted for government, and a mainframe dating from 1982. They run in parallel and together administer the core programs. Every attempt to retire the mainframe has been abandoned or has failed.
Two time axes are standard. This design carries a third, and it exists because the new system inherits fifteen years of records from systems that are still running.
Type the amount into the mainframe by hand.
Valid time
Vendor support for the current platform is committed through at least December 2037, on a rolling ten-year basis.
Version number and the archived binary
Volumes are not yet measured. Caseload throughput, worker streams, transaction rates and queue depth can all be counted directly; the figures here were taken from the technical design documents instead.

We were wrong about the world
We were wrong about the world.
What 326 service-delivery procedures show about how the work is actually done.
What a parameter is
What happens next is well documented. A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal have almost nothing in common beyond involving a person. Making them share a lifecycle means every change to one is negotiated with everyone else. Multiply that over dozens of programs and the model becomes something nobody can change. So sub-entities get bolted on and extended, and integration patterns multiply. The system becomes a plate of spaghetti: nothing can be changed in one place, and any failure reaches everywhere. This is not hypothetical. ICM merged its final two phases and cut child protection scope for exactly this reason.
